Tlepolemus was a key hetairoi of Alexander the Great, playing a crucial role in the governance of the Parthians and Hyrcanii. He was appointed satrap of Carmania by Alexander in 323 BC and retained the position after Alexander's death in 323 BC. Tlepolemus was also involved in the governance of the province of Bactria during the reign of Antigonus I Monophthalmus. He was a member of the coalition formed by Antigonus I Monophthalmus to resist the invasion of Seleucus I Nicator. Tlepolemus's appointment as satrap of Carmania was a strategic move to secure Alexander's border with the Persian Empire. This appointment had significant consequences for the region, as it led to the establishment of a stable satrapy and the preservation of Greek culture in the region. Tlepolemus's legacy can be seen in the continued influence of Greek culture in the region, which persisted for centuries after his death. Despite his significant role in the governance of the region, Tlepolemus remains a relatively obscure figure in historical records, highlighting the complexities of documenting the lives of minor officials in ancient Greece.

Tlepolemus was born into a noble family and received a traditional education, which included training in arms and administration. He was appointed to the position of hetairoi by Alexander the Great, who valued his loyalty and military prowess. Tlepolemus's appointment as satrap of Carmania was a reward for his service to Alexander, and it marked the beginning of a long and distinguished career in the governance of the region.

Tlepolemus's death in 360 BC marked the end of an era in the governance of Carmania, and his legacy continued to shape the region for centuries after his death.
